Assignment 5 – RealNVP on the Two Moons Dataset¶

Akshu Karki

For this assignment I built a RealNVP normalizing flow that learns to turn the two moons dataset (from sklearn.datasets.make_moons) into a plain 2D Gaussian, and back again. I started from the textbook code in notebooks/06_normflow/01_realnvp/realnvp.ipynb (Generative Deep Learning, 2nd ed., Chapter 6) and made a few changes:

  • trained for 600 epochs instead of the 300 used in the book
  • small fixes so it runs on my setup (TensorFlow 2.20 / Keras 3)
  • added a quick check that the flow is actually invertible and that the log-determinant is right
  • I kept the loss history so I could plot the training curve at the end
In [1]:

0. Parameters¶

Same values as the book except for the number of epochs.

In [2]:
COUPLING_DIM = 256
COUPLING_LAYERS = 2
INPUT_DIM = 2
REGULARIZATION = 0.01
BATCH_SIZE = 256
EPOCHS = 600

1. Load the data¶

30,000 points from make_moons with a bit of noise. I normalize them first so each coordinate has mean 0 and variance 1, which puts the data on roughly the same scale as the standard normal we want to map to.

In [3]:
data = datasets.make_moons(30000, noise=0.05)[0].astype("float32")
norm = layers.Normalization()
norm.adapt(data)
normalized_data = norm(data)

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 4))
plt.scatter(
    normalized_data.numpy()[:, 0],
    normalized_data.numpy()[:, 1],
    c="green",
    s=1,
)
plt.title("Normalized two moons data")
plt.show()

2. Build the RealNVP network¶

Coupling layer¶

The coupling layer takes the (masked) input and outputs two things:

  • s (scale): a stack of four Dense(256, relu) layers ending in a Dense(2, tanh). The tanh keeps the scale from getting too large, since it gets exponentiated later.
  • t (translation): a separate stack of four Dense(256, relu) layers ending in a Dense(2, linear).

The two stacks don't share any weights, which is what the assignment asked for. Only difference from the book here is shape=(input_dim,), because Keras 3 wants a tuple.

In [4]:
def Coupling(input_dim, coupling_dim, reg):
    input_layer = layers.Input(shape=(input_dim,))

    # scale network
    s_layer_1 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(input_layer)
    s_layer_2 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(s_layer_1)
    s_layer_3 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(s_layer_2)
    s_layer_4 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(s_layer_3)
    s_layer_5 = layers.Dense(
        input_dim,
        activation="tanh",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(s_layer_4)

    # translation network
    t_layer_1 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(input_layer)
    t_layer_2 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(t_layer_1)
    t_layer_3 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(t_layer_2)
    t_layer_4 = layers.Dense(
        coupling_dim,
        activation="relu",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(t_layer_3)
    t_layer_5 = layers.Dense(
        input_dim,
        activation="linear",
        kernel_regularizer=regularizers.l2(reg),
    )(t_layer_4)

    return models.Model(
        inputs=input_layer, outputs=[s_layer_5, t_layer_5]
    )


Coupling(INPUT_DIM, COUPLING_DIM, REGULARIZATION).summary()

RealNVP model¶

This is a custom Keras Model. It has two coupling layers with alternating masks ([0,1] then [1,0]), so each coordinate gets transformed by the other one at some point.

  • training=True runs data → latent (the inverse direction, used for the loss)
  • training=False runs latent → data (used for generating samples)

The loss is the negative log-likelihood: log p(z) under a standard normal, plus the log-determinant of the Jacobian. Because of the coupling-layer trick, the log-det is just the sum of the s values.

In [5]:
class RealNVP(models.Model):
    def __init__(
        self, input_dim, coupling_layers, coupling_dim, regularization
    ):
        super().__init__()
        self.coupling_layers = coupling_layers
        self.distribution = tfp.distributions.MultivariateNormalDiag(
            loc=[0.0, 0.0], scale_diag=[1.0, 1.0]
        )
        self.masks = np.array(
            [[0, 1], [1, 0]] * (coupling_layers // 2), dtype="float32"
        )
        self.loss_tracker = metrics.Mean(name="loss")
        self.layers_list = [
            Coupling(input_dim, coupling_dim, regularization)
            for i in range(coupling_layers)
        ]

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [self.loss_tracker]

    def call(self, x, training=True):
        log_det_inv = 0
        direction = 1
        if training:
            direction = -1
        for i in range(self.coupling_layers)[::direction]:
            x_masked = x * self.masks[i]
            reversed_mask = 1 - self.masks[i]
            s, t = self.layers_list[i](x_masked)
            s *= reversed_mask
            t *= reversed_mask
            gate = (direction - 1) / 2
            x = (
                reversed_mask
                * (
                    x * tf.exp(direction * s)
                    + direction * t * tf.exp(gate * s)
                )
                + x_masked
            )
            log_det_inv += gate * tf.reduce_sum(s, axis=1)
        return x, log_det_inv

    def log_loss(self, x):
        y, logdet = self(x)
        log_likelihood = self.distribution.log_prob(y) + logdet
        return -tf.reduce_mean(log_likelihood)

    def train_step(self, data):
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            loss = self.log_loss(data)
        g = tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_variables)
        self.optimizer.apply_gradients(
            zip(g, self.trainable_variables)
        )
        self.loss_tracker.update_state(loss)
        return {"loss": self.loss_tracker.result()}

    def test_step(self, data):
        loss = self.log_loss(data)
        self.loss_tracker.update_state(loss)
        return {"loss": self.loss_tracker.result()}


model = RealNVP(
    input_dim=INPUT_DIM,
    coupling_layers=COUPLING_LAYERS,
    coupling_dim=COUPLING_DIM,
    regularization=REGULARIZATION,
)

3. Train for 600 epochs¶

Adam with learning rate 1e-4, same as the book. The callback saves a 2x2 snapshot every 100 epochs (the book does every 10, but with 600 epochs that would be 60 plots, way too many).

In [6]:
model.compile(optimizer=optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=0.0001))


class ImageGenerator(callbacks.Callback):
    def __init__(self, num_samples):
        self.num_samples = num_samples

    def generate(self):
        # data -> latent
        z, _ = model(normalized_data)
        # latent -> data
        samples = model.distribution.sample(self.num_samples)
        x, _ = model.predict(samples, verbose=0)
        return x, z, samples

    def display(self, x, z, samples, title=None, save_to=None):
        f, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2)
        f.set_size_inches(8, 5)
        panels = [
            (
                axes[0, 0],
                normalized_data,
                "r",
                "Data space X",
                "x_1",
                "x_2",
            ),
            (axes[0, 1], z, "r", "f(X)", "z_1", "z_2"),
            (
                axes[1, 0],
                samples,
                "g",
                "Latent space Z",
                "z_1",
                "z_2",
            ),
            (axes[1, 1], x, "g", "g(Z)", "x_1", "x_2"),
        ]
        for ax, pts, c, t, xl, yl in panels:
            pts = np.asarray(pts)
            ax.scatter(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1], color=c, s=1)
            ax.set(
                title=t,
                xlabel=xl,
                ylabel=yl,
                xlim=[-2, 2],
                ylim=[-2, 2],
            )
        if title:
            f.suptitle(title)
        plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.3, hspace=0.6)
        if save_to:
            plt.savefig(save_to, dpi=120, bbox_inches="tight")
        plt.show()

    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        if epoch % 100 == 0 or epoch == EPOCHS - 1:
            x, z, samples = self.generate()
            self.display(
                x,
                z,
                samples,
                title=f"Epoch {epoch + 1}",
                save_to="./output/generated_img_%03d.png"
                % (epoch + 1),
            )


img_generator_callback = ImageGenerator(num_samples=3000)


# printing every epoch gives 600 lines, so just print every 50
class PrintLoss(callbacks.Callback):
    def on_epoch_end(self, epoch, logs=None):
        if epoch == 0 or (epoch + 1) % 50 == 0:
            print(
                f"epoch {epoch + 1:>3}/{EPOCHS}  loss = {logs['loss']:.4f}"
            )

history = model.fit(
    normalized_data,
    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,

)

Sanity check¶

Before looking at the results I wanted to make sure the model is doing what it's supposed to. Two things should be true for a normalizing flow:

  1. going data → latent → data should give back the exact same points (it's invertible)
  2. the log-determinant the model returns should match the real Jacobian. I computed the real one with tf.GradientTape.batch_jacobian and compared.
In [8]:
x_check = normalized_data[:1000]
z_check, logdet = model(x_check, training=True)
x_back, _ = model(z_check, training=False)
print(
    "max reconstruction error:",
    float(tf.reduce_max(tf.abs(x_back - x_check))),
)

x_var = tf.Variable(x_check[:5])
with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
    z_var, _ = model(x_var, training=True)
jac = tape.batch_jacobian(z_var, x_var).numpy()
true_logdet = np.log(np.abs(np.linalg.det(jac)))
for a, b in zip(true_logdet, logdet[:5].numpy()):
    print(
        f"log|det J| from autodiff = {a:.5f}   from model = {b:.5f}"
    )

5. Final results¶

In [10]:

6. Results and comparison with the book¶

Sanity check¶

Both checks passed. Going data → latent → data gives back the original points with a max error of about 2e-6, which is just float32 rounding. The log-determinant from the model matches the one from the real Jacobian to 5 decimal places. So the model is a proper invertible flow and the loss is being computed correctly.

Loss curve¶

The loss (negative log-likelihood) drops really fast at the start. It goes from 2.56 after the first epoch down to 1.77 by epoch 10. After that it's a very slow grind: 1.707 at epoch 100, 1.702 at epoch 300, and 1.695 at epoch 600 (the lowest was 1.694 at epoch 584). So almost all of the learning happens in the first 20–30 epochs and the rest is small improvements.

In the zoomed-in plot you can see it's still going down a tiny bit at the end, so the model hadn't completely stopped improving. But going from epoch 300 to 600 only lowered the loss by about 0.007, which is really small. The curve is also a bit spiky. I think that's because the loss is just the average over the batches in each epoch, and Adam still bounces around a little near the minimum even with a small learning rate (1e-4).

What the plots show¶

  • Epoch 1: f(X) still basically looks like the moons, just bent around. The generated samples g(Z) are a blurry diagonal blob and don't look like moons at all.
  • Epoch 101 / 301: the model has mostly figured it out. g(Z) clearly shows two moon shapes. Epoch 301 is where the book's code would stop (it uses 300 epochs).
  • Epoch 600: honestly it looks almost the same as epoch 301. I couldn't really tell them apart without the titles.

The result isn't perfect though. If you look at f(X), the data doesn't turn into one round Gaussian blob. It turns into two blobs (top and bottom) with an empty gap around z_2 ≈ 0, plus some thin streaks going out to the sides. But when we generate, we sample from a full Gaussian, so lots of samples land in that gap region. The model still has to map them somewhere, and they end up as the line of points connecting the two moons in g(Z). The moons are also a bit thicker and messier than the real data.

Comparing with the book¶

My code is the book's code (same Coupling layer, same RealNVP class, same 2 coupling layers, same hyperparameters, same 30,000 points). The only real difference is the number of epochs, so my epoch-300 snapshot is what the book's setup gives. Just like in the book, f(X) gets pushed towards a Gaussian and g(Z) turns Gaussian noise into two moons. The extra 300 epochs only improved the loss from 1.702 to 1.695, and the pictures basically didn't change. So for this model, training longer than the book doesn't really help.

The book says its code is adapted from the Keras RealNVP tutorial (https://keras.io/examples/generative/real_nvp). That version is almost the same model but uses 6 coupling layers instead of 2, and only trains for 300 epochs. Its results look cleaner than mine. The latent space is a round Gaussian cloud, the generated moons have no bridge between them, and the loss gets down to around 1.2–1.3 (it trains on 3,000 points with a validation split, so it's not an exact comparison, but it's the same kind of loss). That makes me pretty sure the gap and the bridge in my results come from the model only having 2 coupling layers, not from too little training. With 2 layers each coordinate only gets transformed once (the masks are [0,1] then [1,0]). That isn't flexible enough to bend two separate curved moons into one round Gaussian.

One more thing I noticed while going through the code: the Dense layers have kernel_regularizer=l2(0.01), but log_loss and train_step never add self.losses to the loss. So the L2 regularization doesn't actually do anything during training, in the book's code or in mine. I left it the same as the book so the comparison is fair.

Conclusion¶

The RealNVP model learned to map the two moons data into a roughly Gaussian latent space and to generate new two-moon samples from Gaussian noise. The sanity checks showed it really is invertible and that the log-determinant is right. Training for 600 epochs worked fine, but almost all of the improvement happened in the first ~30 epochs, and the result at 600 epochs looks basically the same as at 300 (the book's setting). The leftover problems (the gap in f(X) and the bridge between the moons) look like a limit of using only 2 coupling layers. If I did this again I would try more coupling layers instead of more epochs.
